newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OPEC can only watch as oil prices slide.
newsitem.headline: OPEC can only watch as oil prices slide.

text.p: OPEC, the geriatric oil cartel, meets this week to mourn a slide in petroleum prices which it appears to have little power to resist.
The Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries has watched helpless as a revenue windfall from a firm market in 1996 was wiped out by a 30 percent slump in prices this year.

Ministerial talks in Vienna are set to leave a leaky quota system unchanged again - since any readjustment would trigger disputes over market share - and simply highlight the 11-member group's impotence in recent years to influence energy prices.
"They've tried everything over the last ten years and it's all failed," said Geoff Pyne at Swiss finance house UBS.

OPEC's response to falling prices will be no different than its reaction at the last gathering in November to a six-year high of $25 for Brent blend. The North Sea crude, a world benchmark, is now worth less than $18 a barrel.

Six ministers are already on the record in support of no change to quotas under OPEC's self-imposed 25.03 million barrel per day (bpd) production ceiling, unchanged for all but Iraq since September 1993.
"I have to keep reminding my clients that OPEC is meeting," said Peter Gignoux, energy desk head at brokers Smith Barney.

Actual OPEC production is at a 17-year high of 27 million bpd. Quota cheating is endemic and overall compliance with official quotas is at an all time low. Prospects of those pumping beyond their mandated limits reining back are poor.
Languishing oil prices may put some bite back into ministerial quarrels at OPEC over quota busting.
"There will be some snarling at each other and some promises to stick to quotas but it won't mean a great deal," said an OPEC official.
Only a core of Gulf producers within OPEC, led by Saudi Arabia, now stick to the allocations that are designed to buoy oil prices.
Saudi Arabia's quota of 8.0 million bpd leaves the kingdom with more than two million of spare capacity and is the cornerstone of what remains of OPEC supply restraint.
The Saudis have suggested no hint yet they might consider abandoning their supply cushion and opening the floodgates.
Cash-pinched populous Third World producers like Venezuela, Nigeria and Algeria already prefer to maximise revenues by running supplies at full tilt, ignoring the consequences for the market.
Rampant quota busting, combined with new flows from producers outside the cartel like Norway and Mexico, look likely to mean even lower prices in the second half of the year.

"The ceiling is even more irrelevant than it was before and OPEC production will continue to increase in the second half of the year," said Pyne at UBS. "While oversupply persists prices will continue to fall."
"OPEC's quotas are no longer relevant. It is additional OPEC output that matters," said London's Centre for Global Energy Studies.

Analysts of the oil market say the flawed quota system will survive the week unscathed, because any attempt to renegotiate new allocations would only provoke a row guaranteed to send markets into a tailspin.
"There's no mechanism open to OPEC whether it be exports, or quotas or production which has any long term meaning in the oil market at all," said Pyne.
Iraq, meanwhile, might easily provide the headline hungry oil trading community with more to chew on than the rest of OPEC combined.

Dealers will be keen to hear the latest from Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed on when Baghdad intends to resume exports under the second phase of its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.
-- Vienna Newsroom +431 713 2002
